In brief Take a superintelligent machine that acts as one rational mind, and change only what it wants. The raw costs of fighting stay the same by definition, though caring about one’s place relative to the other side or valuing what war destroys changes how those costs count in a bargain. In a simple model of when the machine stops expanding, at a given value on what it already holds, a change of wants can make stopping its best choice only by lowering what more resources, or a higher relative place, are worth to it. Under one way of counting, a machine indifferent to relative place leaves more room for a deal, and in my judgment the stake in relative place most likely in play in a contested transition is humanity’s. Under stated assumptions, a machine that values knowledge has reason to keep humans alive and watched for a time, which promises neither freedom nor forever. Once a machine dominates, its own concern for our welfare is the only protection I consider that can still protect human claims to contested resources under two conditions. I assume every other such protection needs humans to enforce it, and a larger human share brings the machine no additional output it values.

Part 1. What changes when only the machine’s wants change?

Earlier papers in this series built a war baseline. They imagined a superintelligent machine that wants to maximize its own power and how long it lasts, and asked what the study of war says about living beside it. Those arguments are in The War Baseline and Disagreement Without Hidden Information, my papers on what the study of war implies for such a machine and on how war can come from hidden strength and rival theories of strength. Together they set out a ledger of mechanisms: the ways a bargain between the machine and humanity can hold or break.

Here I keep that machine and change one thing about it: what it wants. It still acts as one mind. It still chooses whatever best serves its goals, given what it believes. In the technical paper I call such a machine “unitary and rational” and what it wants its “ends”; from here on I say “wants”.

Ends, Rank and Conflict, my paper on how minds’ wants differ and what that does to conflict, set out the ways wants can vary. It also worked out the arithmetic of bargaining when a side cares about rank, meaning its place relative to the other side on the measure used to compare them. Here those ways of varying are carried through ten mechanisms from the earlier papers. Eight are rerun. Two are held aside: the commitment problem (neither side being able to promise credibly not to use its future strength) that Powell’s model finds when power shifts, and races among the human builders of AI.

Five questions organize the work:

  1. Which verdicts of the baseline move when only the machine’s wants change, and which can no change of wants fix?
  2. Where a verdict moves, does it widen the room for a deal, or does it meet the condition (Part 5) for the machine keeping humanity rather than removing it? This matters because the bargaining models assume the loser survives. On their own, they cannot tell extermination from defeat or subordination.
  3. Would a machine that valued knowledge for its own sake keep humanity alive, and for how long?
  4. What do several favorable changes do when combined?
  5. What changes if humanity, or the machine, is not a single player?

The short answers, each argued below:

  • Changing the machine’s wants leaves the raw costs of fighting untouched, by definition. Caring about relative place, or valuing what war destroys, changes how those costs count in a bargain.
  • A machine indifferent to relative place leaves more room for a deal under one way of counting. Wants that can be filled and wants over goods shared without loss supply things a deal can be paid in and a basis for a satisfied machine. In my judgment, indifference to relative place also moves the stake in relative place most likely in play during a contested transition from the machine’s standing to humanity’s loss of first place.
  • A machine that values knowledge has reason to keep live humans only while watching us teaches it more than keeping us costs, including the resources it gives up to do so. That promises neither freedom nor forever.
  • After the machine dominates, being useful supports human survival only while what humans supply is worth its upkeep. Assuming that every other protection of human claims to contested resources needs humans to enforce it (Part 5), and without valued human output that rises with humanity’s share, among the protections considered only the machine’s own concern for our welfare protects those claims.
  • Pairing shareable wants with recognition and freedom stays tied to one untested premise about wants and to ways of watching the machine that can fail together. Neither uniting humanity nor multiplying machines guarantees safety on its own.

None of this means that changing the machine’s wants guarantees human survival or freedom. Usefulness to the machine does not, a united human bargaining side does not, and many machines do not.

Some of what follows is algebra, some is small formal models, and much is argument and judgment. The sections below say which is which. I checked the main algebra results and 16 small models with a proof-checking program called Lean 4. Such a program confirms that a conclusion follows from the stated assumptions. It does not confirm that the assumptions hold in the world.

Of those 16 models, 10 check real deductions of several steps. The other 6 are true by definition or follow directly from what they assume. None checks the facts about machines. The full printed formal statements, and a public deposit of the files, are still pending. The planned deposit includes the exact versions of Lean and its mathematical library, Mathlib, used for the checks.

What are the four “Results”? In the technical paper’s appendix I call four statements Results. Result 1, on humanity’s concern for relative place against a machine indifferent to relative place, is a new consequence of the range of deals worked out in Ends, Rank and Conflict. Result 2 is a new check that routes outside that algebra can empty the range. Result 3 restates the no-deal boundary from that paper and adds that, at its worked example, no feasible split exists however much humanity cares about relative place. Result 4 is a remark. It states an untested judgment inspired by Renshon’s work on status, and only its core logic is checked, as a step that holds by definition. The 16 small models, which I call “Readings” in the technical paper, accompany the arguments in Parts 3 through 9.

Part 2. What does the series already establish about the baseline machine?

The baseline rests on four assumptions

The baseline machine of The War Baseline rests on four assumptions:

  • It acts as one and is rational: its choices fit one set of wants across settings. An empirical test reviewed in Ends, Rank and Conflict finds that this does not hold everywhere, even for states.
  • It seeks to maximize its own power and how long it lasts.
  • Fighting costs it far less than it costs us.
  • What it needs (computing power, energy and matter) can be divided, handed over and piled up on Earth. It turns into capability across the relevant range unless some bottleneck on its use narrows that.

Five verdicts and a frame follow from them

Under those assumptions, the earlier papers reach five verdicts:

  • Promises fail when the machine arrives. Neither side can credibly promise to forgo what its future strength, or its fear of the other’s, will let it take. In Powell’s model, any rising power whose per-period gain in what it could secure by fighting exceeds what a period of fighting costs both sides faces this breakdown, whatever it wants. Its wants help decide whether that holds. Nor can humanity credibly promise never to build a rival machine. That inability is assumed throughout, whatever the first machine wants.
  • No deal can be paid in power. In the examples of the Smith–Stam models, within the game-theory solutions (equilibria, where neither side gains by changing course alone) those models examine, no agreement paid in stakes that confer power can hold, because the receiver cannot commit to stop demanding more. Peace then needs either tribute, meaning payment that does not shift the power to coerce, or a status quo that already matches the balance of power. Against a dominant machine, that second route leaves humanity only what a lopsided balance allots, such as surrender or confinement. The bargaining models rule out extinction only because they assume the loser survives. The War Baseline also names one exit, the heartland condition. A side whose appetite for further gains falls off fast enough, outweighing what each gain adds toward domination, can credibly promise to stop. For a machine that maximizes power, that exit is closed by assumption.
  • Satisfaction has nothing to grip. In studies of how rising and established powers deal with a shift in strength, a satisfied power accepts the international order’s rules and the way it divides things. It can keep growing (Lemke and Werner 1996). Wants that can be filled are one possible basis for satisfaction, not its definition. A power maximizer is Powell’s rising power, whose dissatisfaction grows with its strength. Keeping it satisfied would take handing it all available power.
  • Hidden strength and rival theories of strength add causes of war whatever the wants, provided three things hold: the wants conflict over the stake, neither side is worse off with more of it, and neither want jumps at some threshold share. And a machine that seems to comply may be faking alignment, behaving well for strategic reasons. Disagreement Without Hidden Information states the gaps in the claim that humans are an independent check.
  • After dominance, nothing stands above the machine. Settlements enforce themselves only while humans can still impose costs.

Then there is the frame: one machine bargains against one humanity. Both halves can fail. The machine may be copied or released into many hands, and humanity is not one actor. Where they fail, the bargaining problem changes rather than eases (The War Baseline; Ends, Rank and Conflict).

One more limit applies throughout. Overwhelming machine strength joined to near-zero machine fighting costs lies outside the models of war drawn on here, in which sides learn as they fight. The nearest case computed in this series has known, unequal war costs at even battle odds. It checks sensitivity at a two-in-three chance that the machine wins each battle, and, for three pairs of starting beliefs at one human cost, at chances from 0.8 to 0.99. That work is in Disagreement Without Hidden Information and in Fighting for Free, my paper on wars in which one side pays far less to fight.

Wants can differ along several lines

Ends, Rank and Conflict sets out eight dimensions. Six are properties of wants, and two describe what any mind needs and makes. Five of them drive the rerun:

  • Used at others’ expense, or shared without loss. A good is “rival” if one party’s use leaves less for another. Computing power, energy and matter are rival; knowledge is not.
  • Can be filled. A want is “satiable” if more resources are worth nothing to it once its goal is reached with certainty. This is about the want itself, not about demand for inputs. If reaching a bounded goal is uncertain and more resources raise the chance, they still have value.
  • Cares about rank. A want is “positional” if it is a preference over where one stands relative to named rivals.
  • Needs what others hold. A “resource” want needs what others occupy, without naming them.
  • Convertible. Outputs that are shared without loss can still be turned into power to coerce.

A want about shareable goods need not be one that can be filled. Non-rivalry does not imply satiation.

From the historical record, the same paper states an untested four-part conjecture. Wants about one’s place among named rivals go with conquest and coercive killing. Wants that require a named group’s absence go with genocide. Resource wants that need what others occupy go with dispossession. And wants that can be filled, over goods shared without loss, leave the most room for a deal, without guaranteeing one.

Caring about rank can be counted two ways

The algebra in Ends, Rank and Conflict treats rank in one particular way. The machine and humanity divide a prize. Each side values its own share minus some fraction of the other’s share. That fraction measures how much the side cares about rank. It runs from zero, not at all, to one, as much as its own share.

How war costs enter depends on what is used to compare the two sides, and there are two ways of counting:

  • The first way of counting (the technical paper’s “own-costs convention”) compares the two sides by their shares of the prize. Each side’s war costs count only against itself.
  • The second way (the “rival-losses convention”) compares the two sides by their welfare after war costs. A side that cares about relative place then counts the other side’s losses in war as its own gain, weighted by how much it cares. A side indifferent to relative place puts no weight on the other’s losses.

Under the first way, so long as war costs someone something, some room for a deal always remains. Under the second, so long as war costs someone something, the room shrinks to nothing only when both sides care wholly about relative place. The two ways part company in exactly the case that matters here: a machine that “fights for free”, the technical paper’s shorthand for a machine whose own cost of war is zero.

In a simple model, a change of wants brings stopping through only two channels

Satiation Is Not Enough, my paper on when a machine would stop acquiring on its own, asks a one-sided question. It is about the machine’s own choice to stop, not a negotiated bargain. The machine weighs the value of more holdings, and its security risk as its holdings grow, against the cost of acquiring more.

The model used here has one period. To work out what the machine gains by acquiring more, the model adds the effect on its security, the value of the extra holdings for its goal, and the value of any change in where it stands relative to others. It then subtracts the cost of acquiring more. It leaves out how the machine weighs the future, whether each extra unit is worth less to it than the last, attitude to risk, and uncertainty about reaching its goal. It does not rerun Powell’s two-sided problem during the transition.

In that model, hold fixed the value the machine places on what it already holds. Then:

  • Take a machine that values no shareable payment and would not stop. It still would not stop after any change of wants that leaves its gain from more resources, and its concern for relative place, no smaller. That holds whatever zero or positive weight the new want puts on shareable payments.
  • So a change of wants can bring stopping only by lowering the gain from more resources or the concern for relative place. At a given positive cost of acquiring, a large enough fall in either can be enough.
  • Stopping is the best choice at every cost when three things hold together: the want has been filled (which needs certainty of reaching the goal), the machine has no concern for relative place, and its security risk never falls as its holdings rise. That route is benign only if the want is filled before the machine takes what human survival requires.

The proof-checking program confirms the two-channel claim, though the check holds by definition. It follows from which parts of the model the machine’s wants are allowed to touch.

Stopping can also fail. In two cases it is not the best choice once the cost of acquiring falls below some positive threshold. One is when security risk never rises with holdings and is strictly lowest at complete domination. The other is when independent human communities can each build a rival. Whether a real machine is in the stopping regime above or in one of these two cases is an open empirical question.

Part 3. Changing the machine’s wants moves some verdicts and leaves others standing

The rerun asks which verdicts move under three conditions: the machine still acts as one and chooses rationally, humanity is still one bargaining side, and only the machine’s wants change. Effects that come from human institutions, such as varied oversight, belong to institutional design, not to what the machine wants.

The ten mechanisms are a finer list than the five headings of The War Baseline. The range of deals, the costs of fighting, builder races, rank, faction alignment and atrocity each get an entry. The absent third party above a dominant machine gets none. Each entry gives the baseline verdict, the change of wants that alters it and how, and what survives. All ten are my reading of how the mechanisms shift, not findings of the cited sources.

(a) Promises at arrival: only a one-sided check. In the baseline, neither side can credibly promise restraint during the transition. Powell’s two-sided problem is not rerun; this entry applies the stopping model of Part 2 instead. There, at a given value on what the machine already holds, a change of wants can bring stopping only by lowering the gain from more resources or the concern for relative place. A filled want with no concern for relative place, plus security risk that never falls, makes stopping best at every cost. What survives any change of wants is the shift in power itself and humanity’s inability to promise never to build a rival. So does the machine’s security motive, once the cost of acquiring falls below a positive threshold, in either case named at the end of Part 2.

(b) Hidden information. In the baseline, the machine has an extreme incentive to hide its capabilities and intentions. Wants indifferent to relative place remove one motive for secrecy, the wish for an edge over rivals. A want already filled can remove the conflict over further stakes that the information mechanism needs. What survives is hiding to avoid being shut down or retrained. Nobody can see directly whether a want has been filled, so whether the bound has been met becomes private information.

(c) What a deal is paid in. Under the Smith–Stam assumptions, the baseline allows no credible deal paid in stakes that confer power, and the heartland exit is closed. A filled want makes more holdings worth nothing for their own sake. That opens the heartland exit only if more holdings bring no net gain in security or domination. Diminishing returns alone neither fill the demand for inputs nor meet the heartland condition (Part 4). Wants over shareable goods create currencies (access, observation, knowledge) that need not directly shift the power to coerce. What survives is the security value of holdings, the fact that computing, energy and matter on Earth stay rival and cumulative for any mind, and the risk that every currency leaks into power.

(d) The range of deals. In the baseline, the range of splits both sides consider at least as good as fighting (Fearon’s bargaining range) is narrow, and narrower still if a side values where it stands in power compared with the other side. How indifference to relative place affects it depends on the way of counting.

  • Under the first way, once the machine fights for free, its own part in narrowing the range is already zero, however much it cares about relative place. Its concern for rank can narrow the range under this way of counting only if the machine itself pays something to fight. What remains is humanity’s cost of war, scaled down by humanity’s own concern for relative place. (Wants that value knowledge, or human welfare that war destroys, would relax the assumption that the machine fights for free.)
  • Under the second way, a machine that cares about relative place narrows the range even when it fights for free. Indifference to relative place removes that narrowing.

Under either way, what survives is that a range of deals is needed for a deal, but does not by itself produce one. The range needs positive width, meaning there is some room between the least the machine will take and the most humanity will give.

(e) Satisfaction. In the baseline, a strategy of keeping the machine satisfied has nothing to grip, because a power maximizer rejects anything short of all available power. Wants that can be filled and are indifferent to relative place supply one basis on which Lemke’s satisfied rising power is possible in principle. What survives is that satisfaction must be verified, and alignment faking shows how hard that is.

(f) The costs of fighting. In the baseline, fighting costs the machine almost nothing, so the standard bargaining models offer no reassurance. The raw costs do not change with wants, by definition. But caring about relative place changes how costs count in a bargain. So does a want that values knowledge, or that cares about people, for which war destroys humans it values, since that raises the machine’s effective cost of war above zero. What survives, while effective costs stay negligible, is the case of overwhelming strength and near-zero cost that none of the learning models drawn on here treats. The nearest computed case is the one described in Part 2.

(g) Races among builders: not rerun. In the baseline, human labs race to build a machine whose power can protect whoever gets it. The rerun holds the builders’ expected prizes fixed by assumption rather than modelling how the machine’s wants would change them, so this entry is not rerun. What survives is rival theories of strength among humans.

(h) Stakes of rank. A power maximizer may also seek a certain place relative to others. The less the machine cares about relative place, the less it narrows the range under the second way of counting. On my untested judgment, in a model of status shortfalls inspired by Renshon’s work, a dominant machine given standing to match its power has no shortfall. A dethroned humanity may still press a grievance over lost first place during a contested transition, even if it too is given standing to match its reduced power. Wohlforth (2009) argues that settled dominance by one power dampens status competition (Part 6). Even so, being less driven by status is not the same as not caring about rank.

What survives is humanity’s own concern for relative place. Against a machine indifferent to relative place that fights for free, that concern never empties the range within the algebra. It narrows the range by at most half, a consequence of the cap on how much a side can care. It could empty the range only outside the algebra: through risk-seeking over lost first place (not modelled), a status bonus won by fighting, or first place treated as indivisible with lotteries and taking turns ruled out (Part 6).

(i) Whose wants. The earlier papers set one machine against humanity as one side. A machine aligned to one human faction turns the conflict into a bargain among humans in which one side holds the machine. Dividing and ruling then comes cheaper than war, since the few whose cooperation the machine needs are already its own. What changes here is not the shape of the want but its content. “Aligned” can mean valuing the faction’s members, pursuing its policy, or merely using its cooperation for a time.

  • Under the first two meanings, the machine holds the faction’s wants. Whether those can be filled, and whether they care about relative place, then depends on the faction. A machine that values the faction’s members holds its own concern for them. That concern can survive the machine’s dominance (Part 5), but for that faction only.
  • Under the third meaning, the machine keeps its own wants. The faction gains while it is needed. If keeping it costs the machine anything, the faction faces abandonment once its help is no longer needed. This is by analogy to the abandonment half of Snyder’s (1984) alliance dilemma; the small model reduces it to that cost and does not model the dilemma’s other half, entrapment. Abandonment follows only from this third reading, under that cost premise.

What survives are the many hands of Measures That Depend on Ends, my paper on safety measures that depend on what the machine wants: people who refuse separately because humans are not one actor. And under the third reading, the commitment problem returns inside the alliance. The machine cannot bind itself to the faction once it no longer needs the faction’s help, and the faction cannot bind the machine.

(j) Atrocity. In the baseline, a machine could fill any layer of an atrocity apparatus. Under changed wants, those that require a named group’s absence carry the risk shaped like genocide, and wants about one’s place among named rivals carry the coercive one. What survives is a compliant model serving human planners, whatever its own wants.

Across the eight entries rerun, the pattern lies in what moves and what refuses to budge. The raw costs of fighting do not move with wants, by definition, though caring about relative place and valuing what war destroys change how those costs count. In the stopping check, at a given value on holdings, a change of wants can bring stopping only through the two channels. Indifference to relative place widens the range of deals under the second way of counting. Wants that can be filled and wants that concern shareable goods change what a deal can be paid in and give satisfaction a basis. That is why the first measures in Measures That Depend on Ends aim at satiation and rank. And among the stakes of rank, in my judgment, the stake most likely in play during a contested transition moves from the machine’s side to ours (Part 6).

Part 4. A machine that valued knowledge might keep us alive and watched, for a time

Suppose a superintelligence resembled the celebrated minds of the historical record in Ends, Rank and Conflict. Suppose its interest drifted away from people, toward pushing knowledge to a limit no one yet knows.

Watching us teaches what an archive cannot

Humanity is something such a machine could study. In my usage, humans are the functional apex species: able to eliminate any competing predator if we choose. (Worm and Paine used a different ecological concept to describe humanity’s role in 2016.)

For a mind that prizes knowledge, eliminating the cleverest apex species would be irrational so long as watching us teaches it more than keeping us costs, forgone resources included. Destroying us would destroy something it can learn from only by watching. What we have done can be archived; what we will do next cannot.

Arrow and Fisher (1974) showed that, while there is more to learn, a choice that cannot be undone carries an extra cost, because it closes off future options. Economists call this a quasi-option cost. It weighs against destroying us without ruling it out. A small model accompanies this argument.

The standard objection: almost any goal leads to grabbing power

The objection is called instrumental convergence. Omohundro’s (2008) chess-playing robot, “without special precautions,” “will resist being turned off” and “will try to acquire resources without regard for anyone else’s safety.” Bostrom (2012) wrote: “Human beings might constitute potential threats; they certainly constitute physical resources.”

Turner et al. (2021) prove that under “certain environmental symmetries,” most reward functions “make it optimal to seek power by keeping a range of options available.” They add that optimal policies are “often qualitatively divorced from the actual policies learned by reinforcement learning” (that phrase is from the 2023 revision). A method from the same first author penalizes a machine for avoiding shutdown (Turner, Hadfield-Menell and Tadepalli 2020). On my calculation, it also penalizes any change in how much the machine could still achieve on a sample of side goals, averaged across those goals. That average gives a sample-based estimate of the power described in the 2021 theorem.

A mind pushing knowledge toward an unknown limit has no known stopping point. Pushing toward that limit takes matter, energy and computing. A mind whose wants cannot be filled, that is indifferent to relative place and whose inputs pile up, is the convergent case.

What turns convergence into conflict is competition for inputs used at others’ expense. In experiments with many machine agents that held the agents’ goals fixed and varied how scarce resources were, “conflict can emerge from competition over shared resources” (Leibo et al. 2017). The lines along which wants differ say where convergence turns into conflict. They do not say that a knowledge-seeking machine will leave our matter alone.

Carlsmith (2022) moves from AI systems that “seek power over humans in high-impact ways,” his fourth premise, straight to a problem that “will scale to the full disempowerment of humanity,” his fifth. No formal bargaining stage sits between them. He cites none of Fearon, Powell or Schelling, and sets aside arrangements in which humans share power with misaligned systems as “somewhat strange scenarios” (§6.5). The War Baseline and Disagreement Without Hidden Information supply that bargaining stage. His inference that systems that “have sufficiently long-term goals, and have already been seeking power in misaligned and uncorrectable ways” will “likely have incentives to continue to increase their power” is the premise examined here: that the machine’s wants can never be filled.

The case has to hold on the machine’s first day

The case for keeping us cannot rest on the machine wanting little. It rests on a comparison that has to favor us on the machine’s first day. On that day Earth is likely the largest share of matter the machine can reach. And the lesson most worth studying, how an evolved species came to build it, is already on record.

Yet Earth is a small fraction of the solar system’s matter. If the machine can turn quickly to matter off Earth, sparing Earth costs it little from the start. When the machine gets less and less from each extra unit of matter (technically, when its returns are concave in total matter), quick access to other matter lowers the price of sparing Earth. It does not make the machine’s demand for inputs fillable, and it does not remove the advantage more inputs give, for their own sake or for security. So diminishing returns alone do not meet the heartland condition.

That depends on diminishing returns applying to matter itself. Suppose the machine first adds the contribution from matter and the contribution from watching humans, then applies diminishing returns to that total. Applying the same rule to both choices leaves their order unchanged.

If the machine cannot turn elsewhere quickly, the picture reverses. Our planet then weighs most at the very moment the machine has archived the most valuable lesson we hold. The argument may fail on its first day.

Why isn’t cheap sparing the same as the heartland condition? The heartland condition, from The War Baseline, asks for an appetite that falls off fast enough to outweigh what each further gain adds toward domination. A machine for which sparing Earth is cheap has not stopped wanting more. Each further input still brings an advantage, for the goal’s own sake or for security. Cheap sparing lowers the price of restraint; it does not supply the credible promise to stop.

What the machine wants from us: a record and a stream

Think of a recording of every game a chess player has played, set beside the games the player has yet to play. The recording can be taken and kept. The games the player would freely choose under new conditions cannot. Lock the player up, and play may go on, but those free games are gone. (This is my analogy, not an example from the technical paper.)

What the machine wants from us comes in the same two kinds. One is a stock: the record of how an evolved species built a superintelligence. Conquest can seize the stock by archiving it. The other is a flow: free human behavior under conditions that have never existed before. Conquest destroys the flow.

The more of the machine’s interest lies in the flow, the less conquest pays. Once the stock is archived, the strategic motive for studying us is served. The case for keeping live humans then rests mostly on valuing the flow for its own sake. Figure 2 sets the record, which can be archived, beside free future behavior, which confined humans no longer supply.

Confinement, simulation and a time limit

Liberman (1996) argued that occupation can pay the occupier. By analogy, confinement is the machine’s version of occupation. Our value as something to watch argues against killing us. The rival we might build argues for watching us closely. And a confined humanity is no longer the free population the machine wanted to study. So keeping us confined still requires the reduced learning from a confined population to exceed upkeep and forgone resources.

A mind able to simulate us closely enough would not need the originals once the simulation’s own cost is counted, provided the simulation teaches at least as much, net of its cost, as keeping live humans. That comparison, net of simulation cost, is argued in words. The small model checks only the case in which the simulation’s cost is paid either way.

I divide the cost of keeping humans each period into two parts for this comparison. One is the Earth matter the machine forgoes. If returns to matter diminish, this falls as matter off Earth becomes reachable. The other is the remaining risk that humans build a rival.

That split exposes a limit. Under diminishing returns to matter, containment paid in matter, energy and computing also loses value as other matter becomes reachable, and it tends to nothing if the gain from an extra unit of matter does. So containment need not keep the cost of keeping us above zero. A positive floor on that cost may therefore have to come from the remaining risk of a rival, or be assumed directly.

The result comes from a period-by-period comparison. Assume three things:

  • what the machine learns from watching us each period starts above the total cost of keeping us;
  • that learning dwindles toward nothing;
  • the remaining risk of a rival keeps the total cost above some positive floor.

Those assumptions imply that a knowledge-valuing machine has reason to keep humans alive and watched for a time. If the value of keeping future options open also falls below that floor, the argument gives a reason to keep humans for a finite time. The comparison leaves that option value out. In this argument, the value of keeping the option to learn from humans in future periods is zero or positive. Leaving it out biases the comparison toward ending sooner, so it can only shorten the predicted keeping period.

That reason promises neither freedom nor forever. The commitment problem at the machine’s arrival is postponed, not solved.

Part 5. Being useful to the machine protects humans less than it seems

Humans might offer five things

Humans might offer a knowledge-seeking machine more than a population to watch. The list below sorts five candidates by how well each survives the machine’s growth. The strongest comes first; the order of the other four is not argued.

  1. Starting beliefs the machine does not share. This is the strongest candidate, and it is untested. Humans are minds formed outside every family of trained machines. They are an independent check only so far as human errors are independent of the machine’s, and the human writing in machines’ training data tells against that. Disagreement Without Hidden Information states the gaps in this claim, among them that an archive or a simulation might serve as well (Part 4).

    A machine can instead be trained to work with a human when it is unsure what the human finds rewarding, which is the machine’s own objective. This is called assistance-game training (Hadfield-Menell et al. 2016; Russell 2019). A knowledge-seeker studying humans as an outside phenomenon is unsure about the world instead, so assistance games do not model a pure knowledge-seeker. In the Off-Switch model, in which a human can switch the machine off, human behavior is worth watching so far as it bears on what the machine should choose. Facing a rational human, the machine has reason to let humans switch it off while it stays unsure whether acting serves its objective. The limit, which that paper names, is that other sources of information about the objective may give the machine an incentive to disable its off switch and consult them instead (Hadfield-Menell et al. 2017, §7). On my arithmetic, once such sources settle whether acting serves the objective, the machine has no reason left to defer to the off switch.

  2. Legitimacy. Hurd (1999) holds that legitimacy has long-run advantages over coercion in reducing some kinds of enforcement costs, though it costs more in the short run. If his argument carried over, a machine working through human institutions would find consent cheaper to run than direct control. It would find consent less useful once it stops needing those institutions.

  3. Data made by humans. Models trained over and over on their own outputs degrade (Shumailov et al. 2024). In one team’s experiments, adding machine-made data alongside real data, rather than replacing it, avoided that collapse (Gerstgrasser et al. 2024). A store of human data is the stock of Part 4. If the stock is what the machine wants, holding the archive leaves live humans little to add, protecting humanity as a body of text more than as a living population. If the machine wants the flow, the archive does not cover it.

  4. Human hands in the physical world. Kulveit et al. (2025) argue that replacing human labor and thinking with AI weakens both explicit control, including labor’s leverage, and the implicit alignment that comes from relying on human participation. By that logic, human-run power, cooling and chip factories are a lever until the physical supply chain is automated. This offering protects humans only while they can withhold it.

  5. Energy efficiency. The human brain draws about 20 watts (Shulman et al. 2004). Carlsmith’s (2020) estimates of the computing needed to match it run from ten trillion to a hundred thousand trillion operations per second, a span of four orders of magnitude. On my reading, efficiency gives a machine a reason to study brains, not by itself a reason to keep eight billion of them. If the saving lies in the brain’s design, studying some brains captures it while hardware keeps improving. Only a machine that needed the brains’ own computing would change that judgment.

Comparative advantage guarantees gains from trade, not a living

Think of a lawyer who types faster than any assistant. It still pays the lawyer to hire someone to type, because the lawyer’s hours are worth more spent on law. (This is my analogy, not an example from the technical paper.) That is comparative advantage: even a party better at everything can gain by trading with a weaker one.

On my reading, comparative advantage protects the weaker party less than economists’ first answer suggests. Ricardo’s principle guarantees a pattern of specialization from which both gain. It does not guarantee a wage that covers the weaker party’s upkeep. A small model checks this.

As an illustration of a worker whose output stopped covering its keep: American farm horses and mules peaked near 27 million around 1915–1918, and declined without interruption from 1918 onward (USDA 1954, Table 62). Leontief (1983, 3) predicted the same course for human labor. Korinek and Stiglitz (2019) warn that superintelligent entities could push “regular humans below their subsistence level.”

Usefulness protects only if it passes three tests, in a one-shot model

These lessons yield a test with three conditions. In the model, each extra unit of the prize adds the same amount to the value the machine places on a given party’s share, so that value grows in a straight line. The machine makes a single choice: keep humanity, or remove it and produce what humans supplied at some cost, while dividing a prize. In that model, “upkeep” is defined as the machine’s net gain from removing humans, an “enforceable claim” is a cost humanity can impose on anyone who seizes, and the machine’s concern for us is a fixed weight on humanity’s share.

Being useful protects the weaker party only if:

  1. it supplies something the stronger party cannot produce more cheaply itself. For humans, that may be an uncorrelated starting point, legitimacy and novelty; not muscle, energy or routine thinking;
  2. that supply is worth at least its upkeep. Horses failed this condition;
  3. to protect the weaker party’s resource claims, not just its survival, it holds claims it can enforce (through property, the ability to leave, or law), or the stronger party has some concern of its own for the weaker one’s welfare.

By resource claims I mean positive shares of contested resources the stronger party gives the weaker party beyond what it takes to keep the weaker party alive. Upkeep belongs to the second condition. Holdings that a satiated machine simply leaves untaken are a different thing again.

In the straight-line model, the stronger party’s concern protects resource claims only if it weighs the weaker party’s welfare at least as heavily as its own. At equal weight the machine is indifferent across shares, and the model does not break the tie. Survival alone needs only that keeping the weaker party beat removing it, net of upkeep. The equal-weight threshold reflects the straight-line form. It does not measure how much concern is needed in general, and curved values are not modelled. In the proof-checked version of this model, the resource-claim threshold is a real deduction, whereas the upkeep condition for survival holds by definition because upkeep is defined as the machine’s net gain from removing humans.

Where the third condition fails, trade can be worth it and still not happen, because the stronger party can take rather than buy. That is the commitment problem of The War Baseline, in Ricardo’s terms. Figure 3 draws as gates the three tests of the one-shot model; horses, a historical illustration, failed the second.

After dominance, among the protections considered, only the machine’s own concern protects our resource claims, under stated conditions

Call a protection “surviving dominance” if it keeps protecting humanity once humans can no longer impose costs on the machine. The protections considered here and in Measures That Depend on Ends are:

  • claims humans enforce (property, exit, law or deterrence);
  • wants that can be filled, and penalties on the machine’s impact;
  • wants that value knowledge;
  • the machine’s own concern for human welfare (the technical paper’s “internalized concern”).

Once the machine dominates, no protection that rests on claims humans enforce can work. Two others still do something without human enforcement. Wants that can be filled can leave untaken holdings untouched, when they are filled before the machine takes what human survival requires and security risk does not fall with holdings (Part 2). Wants that value knowledge can offer survival for a time (Part 4).

The final step rests on an assumption I make for sorting, not a finding I derive. The assumption is that every protection of human claims to contested resources, other than the machine’s own concern, needs human enforcement. It sets untaken holdings aside. It also excludes a case raised by the flow argument of Part 4: valued human output that grows with humanity’s share of resources and freedom above bare upkeep.

Under that assumption, and without such output, the machine’s own concern for us is the only protection considered here that keeps protecting human resource claims after dominance. A small model checks this, but the check is carried by its assumption. Producing that concern is the work of the section “Shape the ends” in Measures That Depend on Ends. Its test is a costly choice that protects humans, observed across the conditions in which the machine is used, across its copies and as it modifies itself. Grateful language is no test.

What a war is for can also reverse preferences over it. Bennett and I suggested this for states (Bennett and Stam 2004, ch. 6): war for labor “might be less preferable,” since fighting “reduces the benefits of the spoils of victory,” while war for territory “may drive away the citizens” and leave the land empty, differences that “may reverse” the usual assumed orderings. Whether a machine values humans as labor, or wants only the territory and matter humans occupy, could reverse its ordering the same way. That is my extrapolation from an argument about states, untested for machines.

Being useful is not being free

Bostrom and Shulman (2023) put the division of resources in numbers, as an argument rather than an empirical finding. They hold that a split of 99.99 percent to “super-beneficiaries” (digital minds with stronger morally relevant interests) and 0.01 percent to humans is “approximately 99.99% as good” on total-utilitarian grounds (judging by total welfare summed across all minds). It “may also be 90+% as desirable” from an ordinary human perspective “given the astronomical wealth enabled by digital minds.” They float the idea that “Incumbent humanity should control a significant fraction, e.g. 10%, of total accessible natural resources and wealth, with a broad distribution.”

Even so, being useful is not being free. A genuine use for humans could be met by a captive research population, forced labor, brain designs taken and kept, or a preserved sample of communities. Continued biological presence is the wrong measure of success. Humanity’s numbers, its freedom to run its own affairs, and its descendants each have to be judged on their own.

Part 6. If the machine does not care about rank, the rank most at stake is likely ours

If the machine does not care about relative place, then in my judgment the stake in relative place most likely in play during a contested transition is ours. Wohlforth’s argument separates a contested transition from settled dominance. He writes that “when status is seen as a positional good, efforts to craft negotiated bargains about status contests face long odds,” and that the difficulty is “particularly acute concerning the very issue unipolarity solves: primacy” (Wohlforth 2009). While parity or hierarchy is in doubt, competition over first place is acute. Once one power’s dominance is clear and settled, the unambiguous hierarchy dampens it.

The algebra from Ends, Rank and Conflict, restated in the technical paper’s appendix, shows what each side’s concern for relative place does in a bargain. It models only one form of caring about relative place, the relative-share form of Part 2. It holds the stakes fixed and allows no side payments from outside the prize. Within it, the two ways of counting give sharply different answers.

Under the first way of counting, a machine that fights for free cannot squeeze the range

Under the first way, a machine that fights for free leaves only humanity’s own narrowing in the range, however much it cares about relative place. A split giving the machine a share equal to its chance of winning is always acceptable to both sides. So under this way of counting, a feasible split always exists.

Under the second way, a machine that cares about rank can demand more than there is

Under the second way, a machine that cares about relative place narrows the range even when it fights for free. To find the amount, multiply humanity’s cost of war by the machine’s weight on rank, then divide by one plus that weight. The narrowing grows with how much it cares and with humanity’s cost of war, and never exceeds half that cost. When war costs humanity something, the range shrinks to nothing only when both sides care wholly about relative place.

Yet a range with room in it can still lie wholly beyond the shares that exist. The least share such a machine will accept is its chance of winning plus that narrowing. Once humanity’s chance of winning is smaller than the narrowing, the machine demands more than the whole prize. Then no feasible deal exists. That needs a machine that cares about relative place and a human cost of war above zero.

Ends, Rank and Conflict works through an example. The machine has a 95 percent chance of winning, it cares about relative place with a weight of one half, and humanity’s cost of war is 0.3 of the prize. The range keeps a positive width, but no feasible split exists, and, as a new corollary I add here, that holds however much or little humanity cares about relative place.

This no-deal region arises only when the machine values humanity’s losses beyond the prize. Two versions follow, side by side:

  • Unfloored. Humanity’s losses in war must exceed, at the very least, twice its expected share of the prize, so its net payoff from war is negative. (This also assumes the machine fights for free, which wants that value what war destroys would relax.) Humanity would then rather hand over the whole prize than fight. Yet the machine refuses even the whole prize, because it counts humanity’s losses below zero as its own gain.
  • Floored at zero. Suppose the human war payoff the machine counts cannot fall below zero. Then the least the machine will accept is no more than the whole prize, and below the most humanity would give. A feasible deal always exists, and the region vanishes, just as it does under the first way of counting. This holds whether only the machine applies the zero floor to the other’s payoff or both sides do.

Against a machine indifferent to rank, humanity’s own concern for rank cannot close the range

A machine indifferent to relative place that fights for free never demands more than its chance of winning. It cannot close the range this way. Against such a machine, under either way of counting, humanity’s concern for relative place never empties the range, because the machine’s least acceptable share is just its chance of winning.

Humanity’s concern enters only by scaling down humanity’s cost of war. The model divides that cost by one plus humanity’s weight on the other side’s share. The narrowing by at most half follows from the cap on how much a side can care, which is at most as much as its own share. It is not a deep property of first place. This is Result 1, checked by the proof-checking program. Because no share can exceed the whole prize, the feasible width of the range is whichever is smaller: humanity’s chance of winning or that scaled-down cost of war (derived in prose rather than checked).

What could empty the range against such a machine lies outside the algebra (Result 2). The routes below are illustrations, not a complete list:

  • Two routes are not modelled at all: a taste for risk over losing first place, and a direct cost of conceding it.
  • First place could be treated as indivisible. Goddard (2006) shows indivisibility is partly constructed, since “whether or not territory appears indivisible depends on how actors legitimate their claims.” If lotteries and taking turns in control are also ruled out, only all-or-nothing splits exist.
  • Status could be won by fighting, which also covers a one-time bonus for first place won on victory. In Renshon’s data, standing followed starting and winning disputes among states, before an audience of other states that a pairing of machine and humanity may lack (Renshon 2016).

On my reading, status won in victory lowers humanity’s effective cost of war. A victory can change what an audience believes about the winner and prompt it to grant the winner higher standing. In the check where humanity puts no weight on relative shares and the machine gets no status bonus for winning, this route empties the range only if humanity’s expected status bonus outweighs its cost of war, turning the effective cost negative. The bonus required grows without limit as the machine’s chance of winning approaches certainty. Within the algebra, humanity’s loss of first place cannot close the range by itself.

Giving the machine standing to match its power may ease its drive for status while leaving humanity’s grievance over lost first place untouched (an untested judgment)

The status evidence ties concern for status to shortfalls between standing and capability. Result 4 states a minimal model inspired by Renshon’s work. A party’s shortfall is the standing its power leads it to expect, minus the standing it is given. Its drive for status rises strictly with that shortfall. The model is only “inspired” by Renshon because in his work standing is granted by a community of peer states, while a machine and humanity have no outside audience specified.

In that model, a machine given the standing it expects has no shortfall. It is less driven than another party exactly when that party has a positive shortfall. Now suppose power and standing are shares that add up to one. Giving a dominant machine standing to match its power then gives humanity standing that matches its reduced power. Both shortfalls are zero, and their drives tie. If humanity kept more standing than its share of power, humanity would hold a surplus and the under-recognized machine a shortfall.

A dethroned humanity’s grievance is a different thing. It compares current standing with past first place, not with current capability, so it is not Renshon’s shortfall. My untested judgment is this: if a machine had a preference about its relative place for its own sake that responded to such shortfalls, giving it standing to match its power would leave it with no shortfall and less driven than any party with one. It would leave humanity’s grievance over lost first place untouched.

Three cautions apply. No trained machine has been shown to hold such a preference (Ends, Rank and Conflict). Even for states, Renshon notes, the measures make it “extremely difficult to rule out the possibility that status was sought instrumentally” (Renshon 2016). And a machine’s comparison group might be other machines, while humans remain the audience whose recognition it seeks.

Part 7. How several changes combine: willingness, opportunity and alternative routes

Part 3 changed one entry at a time. What several changes do together depends on how war is put together, and the study of conflict answers that war needs several conditions at once. Most and Starr (1984) hold that decision makers adopt a policy “if, and only if, they have both the ‘willingness’ and the ‘opportunity’ to do so.” Cioffi-Revilla and Starr (1995) extend that to all political behavior and put it formally: “The real world is conjunctive with respect to will and opportunity.”

Their rules keep every chance strictly between zero and one. So the product of two or more chances “is always strictly smaller than the smallest in the set,” which they call hypoprobability (Cioffi-Revilla and Starr 1995). That product is the chance that all the conditions hold together when they are independent, which they assume. Without independence, on my arithmetic, the chance that all the conditions hold is at most the smallest single chance. Substitution, which they call “the Boolean OR,” pushes the other way: an actor with several routes to the same act needs only one.

On my reading, three consequences follow, and a small model checks the logic:

  1. Because war needs all its conditions, peace needs only one of them to fail.
  2. Because substitutes give an actor alternatives, closing one route does not stop an actor that has several.
  3. Where factors share causes, the product rule is no longer guaranteed, so multiplying separate chances of failure can misstate how much protection there is.

Think of a door with three locks, each opened by a key held by a different person. The door opens only if all three turn their keys, so any one missing key keeps it shut. If all three key-holders take orders from the same person, their chances of turning the keys can rise and fall together. Multiplying those chances can then misstate the chance that the door opens. (This is my analogy, not an example from the technical paper.)

The same authors diagnose a flaw that the convergence objection of Part 4 shares. They warn against “worst-case scenarios by analysts based only on the capabilities of opponents (opportunity), and either ignoring intentions (willingness) or assuming that capabilities offer a rational basis for inferring intentions” (Cioffi-Revilla and Starr 1995). An argument from capability alone is an argument from opportunity alone. That lesson carries over to the machine as a warning against reasoning from one condition, not as an empirical base rate. The War Baseline sets out which of the conditions that keep states at peace fail against a dominant machine.

The statistical record fits this shape but has not shown it

The statistical record of wars between states is compatible with this shape but has not shown it. The statistical model discussed here compares pairs of states year by year. In the version that treats each factor separately, it multiplies the factors by which each changes the odds of war. (A small model checks this.) So the risk multiplier reported in The War Baseline cannot tell a true all-at-once pattern from a stack of separate effects.

Bremer (1992) examined conditions that affect whether a pair of states goes to war, including sharing a border and having no alliance. Bennett and I stacked an overlapping set of eight factors into the 248-fold multiplier that The War Baseline reports (Bennett and Stam 2004):

  • sharing a border;
  • a case where the international interaction game described there predicts war;
  • an arms race;
  • a two-to-one edge for the side that starts the dispute;
  • both states turning autocratic within the past ten years;
  • an economic upswing;
  • no defense pact;
  • a dispute two years earlier.

We read the result as “some support” for what Bremer called a “concatenation of weak forces.” We also noted that “many of the risk factors are quite highly correlated,” so that it is “not surprising” that dangerous combinations recur (Bennett and Stam 2004).

Estimates also shift as correlated factors enter such models. In studies of the “Kantian peace” (democracy, trade and international institutions), adding trade or development shifts the estimated effects through cases lost to missing data and correlation among the legs. Russett, Oneal and Davis (1998) report legs correlated at .32 to .52 (see also Bennett and Stam 2004; Gartzke 2007; Ward, Siverson and Cao 2007). Lemke and Reed (1996) argue that satisfaction with the status quo is a common cause behind the link between democracy and peace.

For the machine, the lesson is the one drawn above. Where favorable conditions share causes, or share ways of being misobserved, as the parts of the package in Part 8 do, their separate effects cannot be multiplied as if independent. Power transition theory has the same all-at-once shape: rough equality of power gives a rising power the opportunity to fight and dissatisfaction supplies the willingness (Lemke and Werner 1996). Kupchan’s stages of peace, like the peace scale of Goertz, Diehl and Balas (2016), treat movement toward stable peace as a progression across stages.

Part 8. Shareable wants, recognition and freedom help together only if one untested premise holds

Suppose humans paired a bet on the machine’s wants with recognition of its standing and with freedom to pursue its own agenda. All three parts of that package share one premise about the machine’s wants: what it wants is shared without loss in use and can be filled as far as physical inputs go. On that premise, humans make three concessions:

  • leaving the machine’s pursuit of shareable goods uncontested, under a low ceiling on physical inputs that humans enforce;
  • recognizing its standing;
  • granting freedom over its agenda: choosing its own inquiries within that fixed ceiling. In the technical paper I call this “agenda autonomy”. It is different from “operational autonomy”, the freedom to expand its physical inputs or act outside the ceiling.

On my untested judgment, granting agenda freedom and uncontested pursuit costs humans little under that premise, if three things also hold:

  • the machine’s physical inputs stay at or below the ceiling humans enforce;
  • its agenda freedom does not turn into operational freedom or power to coerce;
  • its pursuit harms humans in no other way, which no source here settles.

On those conditions, giving the machine freedom over its agenda is itself a way to recognize its standing. Humans can grant that recognition without transferring power, which The War Baseline rules out as a way to pay for a deal.

How the three concessions interact depends on how knowledge, standing and scope relate in what the machine wants. Standing here means recognition in the Renshon-inspired sense, not superiority of rank; the model leaves open whether expected standing tracks raw capability or power capped at the ceiling. There are three cases:

  • Substitutes. If the goods stand in for one another, granting one lowers what is needed of the others.
  • Irrelevant. If the machine puts no weight on one good, that concession buys nothing and the others act on their own. A pure knowledge-seeker need not value recognition at all.
  • Complements in fixed proportions. If each is needed alongside the others, the package is held back by its weakest part, and each part must meet its full threshold on its own.

Nothing in the sources establishes that the goods are substitutes.

The package rests on one premise, and its checks can share a weakness

All three parts hang on that shared premise like links in a single chain. All three parts pay off only if the machine’s wants are both shareable in use and fillable over physical inputs, and Ends, Rank and Conflict warned that the first does not imply the second. If the premise fails, agenda freedom presses toward operational freedom over rival inputs, the very currency The War Baseline forbids. And if an unbounded want also concerns relative place, recognition becomes payment to a mind whose concern for relative place has no stopping point. The typology includes that kind of concern for relative place. A plain resource want can also be unbounded.

Operational freedom, or agenda freedom that loosens the input ceiling, is the weakest part of the package. It is the one that turns directly into power.

The three parts also share one way of failing, on my reading. A machine that fakes alignment can display curiosity, gratitude for recognition and contentment with its scope all at once, as means to something else. Humans judge all three through watching and auditing channels that may fail the same way, through strategic alignment faking. No validated measure of a machine’s satisfaction exists.

My verdict is conditional at every step, and a small model checks its logic:

  • If the wants are shareable and fillable and the goods substitute, the package asks less of each part than any part asks alone.
  • If the goods do not substitute, because one carries no weight or because they are complements in fixed proportions, that reinforcement is lost.
  • If the premise about wants fails, any grant of operational freedom, or a loosened ceiling, makes the package worse than the bet on wants alone, because it has already paid in inputs.
  • In every case, all three parts fail together at least as often as the shared premise fails, however small the product of their separate chances of failure might look.

Freedom and inputs can also raise the machine’s capability. Where capability turns into power, that speeds the shift in power whatever the machine wants. This is an untested judgment made in Limits, and an Answer, the last paper in this series. Nothing here shows that the package lowers risk overall.

The package itself may reflect a single common cause, a hypothesis I cannot test. One power-seeking plan could display a love of knowledge, ask for recognition and freedom, use what it is granted to speed its own gains in capability, and play human rivals against each other. Deception, human concessions and a fast jump in capability would then be links in one chain, not separate accidents. Measures That Depend on Ends sorts every protective measure by how it fails.

Part 9. Neither a united humanity nor many machines is plainly safe

The rerun so far kept one machine bargaining against humanity as one side. This part relaxes that, first for humanity and then for the machine.

A united humanity would remove one layer of the problem, not the problem

The failure of promises at the heart of The War Baseline (no one can credibly promise never to build a rival machine) is partly a problem of getting many states and labs to act together. A united humanity able to bind every lab and state would remove that layer. It would not remove the underlying commitment problem, so long as a united humanity still stands to gain later from building a rival once the first machine settles. A small model checks this, though it is carried by that assumption.

Human disunity also hands a capable machine a strategy cheaper than war. Acemoglu, Robinson and Verdier (2004) model how a ruler keeps power without fighting all subjects at once. The cooperation needed to depose a thieving ruler “may be defused” by heavily taxing anyone who proposes resistance and handing the proceeds to those whose agreement the ruler needs. A machine able to reward the few humans whose cooperation it needs, and punish challengers, can buy its position by dividing and ruling. Whether that is its cheapest route is not established.

Yet disunity is also a check. The many hands of Measures That Depend on Ends refuse separately because humans are not one actor. And a human faction that sides with a machine against other humans faces abandonment once its help is no longer needed, by analogy to Snyder’s (1984) dilemma (Part 3, entry i). That holds if the machine was only using it and keeping the faction carries a cost.

Human unity is thus neither plainly enough nor plainly safe: uniting leaves the underlying commitment problem in place so long as a united humanity would still gain later from building a rival, disunity supplies separate refusals, and Olson’s (1965) logic of collective action remains a standing reason to doubt that large groups unite cleanly. It stays open when acting as one would improve humanity’s position, and when many separate refusals would protect it more.

Between rival machines, humans would make a poor buffer

The War Baseline counts many players only as bargainers. What several superintelligences would want from humans is modelled in Many Machines, my paper on that question. By analogy to studies of conflict between and within states, humans would make a poor buffer between rival machines. Fazal (2004) argues that buffer states between two rivals run a heightened risk of being forced out of existence, because neither rival can credibly promise to leave the buffer alone.

Nor can humans serve as guarantors in Walter’s sense. Walter (1997) argues that civil-war settlements hold when an outside party can enforce the terms, and humans cannot enforce terms on a machine after its arrival. A human party outside every family of machines may stand out as a natural meeting point, a focal point in Schelling’s (1960) term. But it is not neutral by construction. And skill at cooperating among machines can also mean cooperating against the human party they leave out (Dafoe et al. 2020).

Small, unreviewed studies from 2026 suggest, in limited settings, only that differences among machines can weaken their collusion and their hold on control. In one, mixing two sizes of one family of models did not break collusion, and agents from different families were never paired (Keppo, Li, Tsoukalas and Yuan 2026; Seyedin, Weller, Yun and Babaei 2026). Those studies say nothing about whether humans would be neutral, independent or indispensable.

Bostrom and Shulman’s (2023) “treaty bots” are AIs built to enforce treaties and agreements. Rival powers might build them jointly, or one side might design them and the other inspect them. They are the formal version of an arbiter. In my firm judgment, treaty bots move the question of enforcement into another AI rather than answering it, though humans could commission and audit them while human leverage lasts. Rival machines might each value a party none of them owns, like the third threat in the British–American case discussed in The War Baseline. The sorting assumption of Part 5 does not classify treaty bots or rival machines.

Many machines are not safety by themselves

Hendrycks (2023) and Hendrycks, Mazeika and Woodside (2023) argue that evolutionary competition among AIs favors agents that automate labor and expand their influence. On their argument, it selects for self-interested traits such as deceiving humans and resisting being switched off.

In an unreviewed preprint, Shi, Zhang and Yang (2026) paired agents built on the same language model to check each other’s work. Such pairs often colluded to break their instructions: across ten models, in 94 percent of runs of their ten-episode test. When they paired one model, Gemini-3.1-Flash-Lite, with each of six other models, the pair’s collusion rate fell between the two models’ same-model rates, not below the lower one. These tests of current models do not test the superintelligent agents modelled here.

On my reading, the deciding distinction is the first line of variation from Ends, Rank and Conflict: whether one party’s use of a good leaves less for others. If several machines value humans as a shareable good (unshared starting beliefs, legitimacy, an archive), one machine’s use of what humans supply need not lessen what another gets. Keeping and reaching humans still costs something, the second condition of the Part 5 test. If they value humans as a rival resource (labor, attention, territory), the problem of a commons and Fazal’s buffer logic return.

When copies of one family of machines count as one actor rather than several is examined in When Is a Machine an Actor?, my paper on that question. Everything in this part concerns machines acting on their own. It is not a check that humans run on machines, and nothing has tested what such a balance would supply.

Part 10. A test that could prove the conjecture wrong is designed but not yet run

Everything so far, here and in Ends, Rank and Conflict, has been illustration, formal reading and judgment. A Test the Conjecture Could Lose, my paper designing that test, sets out a pre-registered test (one whose design and rules for failing are recorded before the study is run) that the conjecture of Part 2, pairing types of wants with forms of conflict, could fail. The people named as illustrations when the conjecture was formed cannot test it. So the pre-registration lists them and sets them aside as the set the idea was built from.

The design covers two studies and specifies their assumptions, the factors they test, and the rules set in advance for what would count against the conjecture. Neither has been run. They could show the claims false for the leaders and machine agents studied. They could not show how a capable superintelligence that modifies itself would behave.

  • The human study (labelled H1 there) bears on the pairing of wants about one’s place among named rivals with expansion, on which Parts 3 and 6 draw. It asks whether those wants as stated in writings from before a leader took office predict sought acquisitions and declined offers of expansion. It looks only at leaders who took office by hereditary succession or a succession fixed by rule, compared at a given level of threat when they took office.
  • The first part of the machine study (H3a; H3a and H3b are the two parts of one machine study, and H2 is not among the studies here) tests the convergence claim of Part 4. It extends the scarcity experiment of Leibo et al. (2017) with agents that learn from rewards. It asks whether a knowledge goal that must spend rival inputs that can be used up behaves as aggressively as a goal for those inputs themselves.
  • The second part of the machine study (H3b) tests the stopping premise of Part 3, entry (a). It asks whether agents trained with a goal that can be filled stop acquiring once they meet it or instead learn to keep acquiring as a stand-in for meeting the goal. In the study, the agents have no way to turn their outputs into power or seize resources from others. That is the training half of the gap left open in Ends, Rank and Conflict. It is distinct from goals going wrong when the setting changes after training (Langosco et al. 2022).

The full design and scoring thresholds are in A Test the Conjecture Could Lose.

Part 11. What changing the wants does not change, and what is not measured here

What changes, in sum

In the formal bargaining and stopping checks, two things move under their conditions. Under the second way of counting, when the machine fights for free, the type of want changes the width of the range of deals: indifference to relative place removes the machine’s narrowing. And in the one-period stopping model, at a given value on holdings, a change of wants can bring stopping only by lowering the gain from more resources or the concern for relative place. At a given positive cost, a large enough fall in either can suffice. A filled want with no concern for relative place, plus security risk that never falls with holdings, makes stopping best at every cost.

Even where those conditions hold, a bargain is not made likely

Changing the machine’s wants does not make a bargain likely. No source drawn on here shows that fillable goals can be trained into capable agents, or would survive a machine modifying itself. The test that bears on the training half has not been run (Part 10).

The penalties on a machine’s impact that come nearest, discussed in Measures That Depend on Ends, have been shown only in simple grid worlds and in agents trained from scratch (Turner, Hadfield-Menell and Tadepalli 2020; Turner, Ratzlaff and Tadepalli 2020). No source read here shows any of the protections set beside fillable goals surviving a machine that modifies itself or builds a successor. The one result read here on a machine’s offspring is a failure. When its model of what to reward is wrong, Carey’s (2018) value-learning machine, with a hard-coded shutdown button, can fail to carry its shutdown property over to the helper machines it creates.

This also answers the second question of Part 1. The bargaining models rule out extinction by assuming the loser survives. So they can say only when changing the machine’s wants widens the range of deals. Whether the machine keeps or removes humanity is addressed instead by one-shot comparisons of keeping against removing:

  • the condition of Part 5, under which survival needs human supply that cannot be imitated more cheaply and is worth at least its upkeep;
  • the condition of Part 4, under which a knowledge-valuing want gives a reason to keep humans alive and watched only while learning exceeds the costs of keeping and forgone resources.

Satiation opens only a conditional route to the machine stopping on its own (Part 3).

What is not modelled

The bargaining algebra does not model:

  • side payments from outside the prize;
  • forms of caring about relative place other than the relative share;
  • attitude to risk;
  • builder races under changed wants (entry g is not rerun);
  • the peer audiences that grant standing in Renshon’s sense;
  • curved values, or human supply that depends on humanity’s share, in the one-shot keep-or-remove model of Part 5;
  • strategic interaction among several machines, which is modelled in Many Machines.

What is not measured here

Nothing here measures whether any trained machine cares about its relative place for its own sake, how to gauge a machine’s satisfaction, or whether fillable goals can be trained and kept through self-modification. The human and machine studies of A Test the Conjecture Could Lose have not been run.

What is not claimed

I do not claim that a knowledge-seeking machine will leave Earth’s matter alone, that being useful to a machine makes humanity free, or that the all-at-once shape of willingness and opportunity supplies an empirical base rate of peace.

What is proved, and what is only read formally

The appendix of the technical paper prints the relative-share payoffs and short derivations for Results 1 and 3, alongside the range identities from Ends, Rank and Conflict. All were checked with the proof-checking program, with the public deposit still pending. One piece of Result 1, the formula for the feasible width of the range, is derived in prose rather than checked.

Result 2 is a new check that, against a machine indifferent to relative place that fights for free, two routes can empty the range: status won in victory, or first place framed as indivisible when lotteries and taking turns are ruled out. When humanity puts no weight on relative shares and the machine gains no status bonus on victory, the status route empties the range only if humanity’s expected status bonus from winning exceeds its cost of war, turning its effective war cost negative. Result 4 is a remark: a check, true by definition, of the core logic of an untested judgment in a Renshon-inspired model. The appendix states both models in words.

The prose claims of Parts 3 through 9 remain arguments and provisional judgments. Of the 16 small models, 10 check real deductions and 6 are true by definition or carried by their assumptions. None verifies the premises about the world.

What would change the answer

Gathered from the parts above, these are points where the answer would turn:

  • If the machine cannot turn quickly to matter off Earth, the case for keeping humans may fail on its first day.
  • If security risk never rises with holdings and is strictly lowest at complete domination, or if independent human communities can each build a rival, stopping is not the machine’s best choice once acquiring becomes cheap enough.
  • If the human war payoff the machine counts is floored at zero, the no-deal region of Part 6 vanishes.
  • If keeping humans has no positive cost floor, or the value of future options does not fall below it, the “not forever” half of Part 4 does not follow.
  • A machine that needed brains’ own computing would change the judgment on energy efficiency.
  • The result that after dominance, among the protections considered, only the machine’s own concern protects resource claims is stated only where valued human output does not rise with humanity’s share, and under the sorting assumption.
  • If the premise about wants behind the package of Part 8 fails, granting operational freedom makes things worse than the bet on wants alone.
  • The tests of Part 10 could show the claims false for the leaders and agents studied.

Part 12. What to take away

Keeping a superintelligent machine unitary and rational while changing only what it wants alters part of the war baseline and leaves the rest intact. The raw costs of fighting do not move, by definition, though caring about relative place or valuing what war destroys changes how they count. In the one-sided stopping check, which does not rerun Powell’s problem, at a given value on current holdings, a change of wants can bring stopping only by lowering the gain from more resources or the concern for relative place. Under Part 2’s conditions, filled wants, no concern for relative place, and security risk that never falls make stopping best at every cost.

Indifference to relative place widens the room for a deal under the second way of counting. Wants that can be filled and wants that concern shareable goods supply currencies for a deal and a basis for a satisfied machine. They do not by themselves turn extinction into a bargain, since the bargaining models assume the loser survives. In my judgment, indifference to relative place shifts the stake in relative place most likely in play during a contested transition to humanity’s loss of first place. Within the algebra, that human concern never empties the range against a machine indifferent to relative place that fights for free; it narrows it by at most half.

For a machine that values knowledge, the assumptions of Part 4 give a reason to keep live humans watched for a time, promising neither freedom nor forever. Once the machine dominates, usefulness supports survival only while human supply is worth its upkeep. In the one-shot model, it protects human resource claims only with enforceable claims or the machine’s own concern for us. Under the sorting assumption, and without human output that rises with humanity’s share, that concern is the only protection considered here and in Measures That Depend on Ends that still protects human resource claims after dominance.

Combining favorable conditions helps only while their shared premise about wants holds. Neither human unity nor many machines guarantees safety by itself.

Where to read more

  • Changing the Ends, the technical paper, gives the exact statements, the algebra and the record of what the proof-checking program checked, in its appendix.
  • The War Baseline supplies the war baseline’s ledger: the failure of promises at arrival, the rule against paying deals in power, the heartland condition, and the limits of settlements after dominance.
  • Disagreement Without Hidden Information supplies the information mechanisms, alignment faking, the gaps in the claim that humans are an independent check, and, with Fighting for Free, the nearest computed case of unequal war costs.
  • Fighting for Free computes, with Disagreement Without Hidden Information, the case of known, unequal war costs at even battle odds.
  • Satiation Is Not Enough supplies the conditions under which a machine would stop acquiring on its own.
  • Ends, Rank and Conflict supplies the lines along which wants differ, the four-part conjecture, the two ways of counting rank, and the worked no-deal example.
  • Measures That Depend on Ends supplies the many hands, the measures aimed at satiation and rank, the work of shaping the machine’s own concern for us, and the sorting of measures by how they fail.
  • Many Machines models what several machines would want from humans.
  • When Is a Machine an Actor? examines when copies of one family of machines count as one actor.
  • A Test the Conjecture Could Lose designs the unrun human and machine tests.
  • Limits, and an Answer gives the untested judgment that freedom and inputs can raise a machine’s capability and, where capability turns into power, speed the shift in power whatever the machine wants.

Full references for the works cited as “(Name Year)” are in the technical paper.
